P1.section: FINDINGS > 1. Post-earnings announcement drift — the original effect
P1.text:
**CLAIM:** PEAD is the longest-surviving and best-documented directional anomaly; sorting on standardised unexpected earnings (SUE) historically produced roughly 2% abnormal return over the 60 trading days following an announcement, with drift persisting two to three quarters.
**SOURCE:** Ball & Brown (1968), *Journal of Accounting Research*; Bernard & Thomas (1989), *Journal of Accounting Research* 27, 1–36; reviewed in Josef Fink, "A Review of the Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift," University of Graz Working Paper 2020-04 (Nov 2020), https://static.uni-graz.at/fileadmin/sowi/Working_Paper/2020-04_Fink.pdf — **peer-reviewed originals, working-paper review**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong (for the historical effect)
**HORIZON:** Drift strongest in the first quarter after announcement; persists 2–3 quarters. Fink reports Bernard & Thomas at ~2% over 60 trading days, ~4% per quarter; early long/short estimates reach ~18% annualised.
**DECAY EVIDENCE:** See finding 2 — substantial.
**DATA OBTAINABILITY:** Excellent. SUE from a time-series model of quarterly EPS is computable **entirely from EDGAR XBRL** (`EarningsPerShareDiluted`, quarterly, 8+ quarters history). Analyst-based SUE needs IBES or a vendor. Fink notes analyst-forecast-based surprises produce *larger* drift than time-series surprises — so the free version is the weaker version.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** The 60-day drift window maps cleanly onto 60–90 DTE contracts. This is the single best horizon fit in the entire literature for this product. The problem is entirely whether it still exists.

---

P2.grade: Weak (methodologically transparent but unrefereed, <4 years, one regime, self-disclosed probable survivorship bias)
P2.text:
**CLAIM:** An independent out-of-sample test over 43,111 announcements from Jan 2023 to Oct 2026 finds PEAD still present in large caps but small and fading fast.
**SOURCE:** Gaurav Gupta, "Is Post-Earnings Drift Still Tradable? 43,000 Announcements, 2023–2026," https://guptagaurav.info/articles/earnings-drift — **practitioner blog post, not peer-reviewed; author discloses AI assistance in the analysis**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Weak (methodologically transparent but unrefereed, <4 years, one regime, self-disclosed probable survivorship bias)
**HORIZON:** Position formed at close of day +1, drift measured days +2 to +61 — i.e. ~3 months. Direct fit to 60–90 DTE.
**DECAY EVIDENCE:** Top-minus-bottom SUE quintile spread, all sizes: +1.7 pp over 60 days (t = 4.2). Large caps (>$10bn): +2.0 pp (t = 3.4). Mid: +1.4 pp (t = 2.9). Small: +1.1 pp (t = 2.1). **But the spread is +2.6 pp for 2023–24 announcements versus +0.5 pp for 2025–26.** The earnings-announcement-return (EAR) variant is weaker and insignificant: +1.3 pp (t = 1.4).
**Net of costs** (mid+large long-short book): gross 7.9%/yr, Sharpe 1.21; 6.0% at 10 bp one-way, 4.0% at 20 bp, 2.1% at 30 bp. Year-by-year at 10 bp: −1.3%, +13.6%, +2.2%, +7.9% — i.e. most of the return came from a single year (2024).
**DATA OBTAINABILITY:** The signal used is YoY change in quarterly EPS scaled by its own 4–8 quarter variability — **computable from EDGAR XBRL alone**, no IBES required.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** The one piece of evidence that PEAD still has a pulse in large caps at the right horizon. Treat it as a hypothesis to re-test, not a result. The 2025–26 collapse to +0.5 pp is the number to watch. Note the internal inconsistency flagged in the source (chart commentary describing a 4→5.4 point gap does not reconcile with the 1.7 pp headline), which is a reason for caution.

---

P3.section: PART 6 — EARNINGS-CYCLE STRUCTURE AT 42–180 DTE > 6.3 The post-earnings window — positive evidence, in the opposite direction to the brief's hypothesis
P3.grade: Strong for the direction (peer-reviewed, explicit offer/bid execution);
P3.text:
**CLAIM:** Straddles bought *after* earnings announcements earn returns more negative than straddles in
firms with no nearby announcement; straddles bought *before* announcements earn about +5.1%; the
long-short portfolio earns about 14.4% over a one-month holding period; combining the announcement-timing
signal with the historical-minus-implied volatility spread raises the hedge return to 29.2% against 13.7%
for the volatility spread alone; and executed at the offer and sold at the bid the two-way strategy still
returns about 14.9% (HV-IV version) and about 9.4% (prior-month volatility version).

**SOURCE:** Sung Gon Chung & Henock Louis, "Earnings announcements and option returns," *Journal of
Empirical Finance*, 2017, 40: 220–235. DOI: 10.1016/j.jempfin.2016.07.010 **[PR]**
The authors attribute the pattern to traders underestimating volatility before announcements (especially
after calm periods) and overestimating it after announcements (especially after volatile periods), and
suggest recency bias as a mechanism. Their stated conclusion is that **post-announcement options appear
expensive** and pre-announcement options appear cheap. They also note single-factor strategies — the
volatility spread alone or announcement timing alone — shrink to small returns after costs.

**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong for the direction (peer-reviewed, explicit offer/bid execution);
Moderate for magnitude in a retail context, because the headline figures are long-short and the
cost-surviving versions are two-way strategies combining both legs.

P4.grade: Moderate (sample of ~5,182 traders using a trading journal — likely more active and sophisticated than typical retail, which the authors note).
P4.text:
**CLAIM:** Retail option trades average −0.9% per trade, option purchases −3.95%, 0DTE trades −4.6%, with median maturity collapsing from four days to one day between 2020 and 2022.
**SOURCE:** Vincent Bogousslavsky & Dmitriy Muravyev, "An Anatomy of Retail Option Trading," 29 Aug 2024. https://www.lsu.edu/business/files/event-files/2025-finance-mardi-gras/retail_option_trading_v2.pdf **[WP]**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Moderate (sample of ~5,182 traders using a trading journal — likely more active and sophisticated than typical retail, which the authors note).
**Details:** Average option trade −0.9% (t = −3.57) including commissions and spread; purchases −3.95%; **naked option sales +20%**; stock trades roughly flat (+0.11%). Small traders lose most per option trade (−3.4%); multi-day traders −0.9%. 0DTE ≈ 23% of option trades, −4.6% average. SPY and SPX ≈ 26% of retail option trades; top ten underlyings ≈ 60%. Median moneyness ~0.97–0.98 (ATM to slightly OTM). The authors note typical option spreads of 5–10%+ while observed losses are much smaller, inferring substantial limit-order use.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** The asymmetry between purchases (−3.95%) and naked sales (+20%) in the same sample is the clearest statement of the structural headwind on long premium. It also confirms the Bakshi–Crosby–Gao direction with real retail trades rather than synthetic portfolios.

P5.section: PART 1 — IS THERE A HARVESTABLE VARIANCE RISK PREMIUM IN SINGLE NAMES AT ALL? > 1.2 The large-sample picture — and it is genuinely conflicting
P5.grade: Strong. Largest sample in the literature, peer-reviewed in a top-three journal.
P5.text:
**CLAIM:** Across roughly 6,000 underlying stocks over 1996–2009, the mean delta-hedged call gain held
to maturity (~50 days) was −1.13% of the initial position (median −1.29%), with 78% of stocks showing
negative average call returns, 32% significantly negative, and only about 1% significantly positive.

**SOURCE:** Jie Cao & Bing Han, "Cross section of option returns and idiosyncratic stock volatility,"
*Journal of Financial Economics*, 2013 (108: 231–249). **[PR]**
https://www-2.rotman.utoronto.ca/facbios/file/Han_JFE_published.pdf
Sample: OptionMetrics, Jan 1996 – Oct 2009; 6,141 call underlyings / 6,065 put underlyings; ~1,514
stocks per month; 213,640 call and 199,198 put observations.

**Cross-sectional dispersion (the central question of this strand), stock-level mean call gains:**

| Percentile | 10th | 25th | 50th | 75th | 90th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean delta-hedged call gain | −3.75% | −1.85% | −0.77% | −0.08% | +0.77% |

**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong. Largest sample in the literature, peer-reviewed in a top-three journal.

**IMPLICATION FOR THE BUILD:** This is the most important table in the strand. Read from the seller's
side, the median name hands a premium-seller +0.77% of the hedged position per ~50 days, the 25th
percentile name +1.85%, and the 10th percentile name +3.75%. **But the top quartile of names pay the
seller essentially nothing (+0.08%) and the top decile pay negative (−0.77%).** So: (a) a premium does
exist on average; (b) it is small at the median; (c) roughly a quarter of the optionable universe is
not worth selling at any cost level. Selection is not an optimisation, it is the whole strategy.

---

P6.text:
**CLAIM:** Retail option traders lose 5–9% of their option investment around earnings on average, and 10–14% for high-expected-announcement-volatility events, with aggregate losses ≈$3bn.
**SOURCE:** Tim de Silva, Eric C. So & Kevin Smith, "Losing is Optional: Retail Option Trading and Expected Announcement Volatility," *Review of Finance* 30, 2026, pp. 489–535 (online Oct 2025). https://www.timdesilva.me/files/papers/losing_optional.pdf **[PEER]**
**EVIDENCE STRENGTH:** Strong.
**Details:** Nasdaq and PHLX clientele-split trade data matched to 32,758 US quarterly announcements, 2010–2021. Retail buys ATM calls in the days before high-EAV announcements; media coverage appears to drive the attention. Market makers absorb the demand; retail purchases raise option-implied variances by **~40%** for top-quintile retail buying. Three loss channels: (1) options overpriced relative to subsequent realized vol — straddles underperform by **~11%** on high-EAV announcement days vs low-EAV and a further **~9%** over the next 10 days, with no reversal; (2) wide pre-announcement spreads costing **~9%** extra on a half-spread assumption; (3) slow closing of losers consistent with the disposition effect. Retail option dollar volume rose from ~$20bn (2010) to ~$240bn (2020). The authors attribute the behaviour to behavioural error rather than hedging, lottery preference, or private information. Transaction-cost estimates assume hold-to-maturity and half-spread, so they are **lower bounds**.
**IMPLICATION FOR THE APP:** Devastating and specific. "News catalyst" is one of the app's four named selection inputs, and the single best-documented systematic retail loss in the options literature is *buying options into a known catalyst*. Retail demand itself inflates the IV by ~40%, and the loss is three-part: overpricing, spread, and failure to exit. If the app ranks contracts higher because an earnings catalyst is approaching, it is mechanically steering users into the configuration with the largest measured retail loss in the literature. The defensible version of a catalyst input is **negative-signed for long premium** and accompanied by an IV-crush warning.

depends_on.why: It is the only claim, and the only finding that carries a direction. Without the earnings beat, nothing points toward a higher close. The other findings carry no direction.

checks_that_are_one_problem.note: Both flags describe the same weakness: the thesis rests on one earnings-beat finding, and that finding is graded moderate rather than primary-source.
Both flags say the chosen 500 call can lose even if the stock closes higher. The breakeven sits well above spot, so the strike fits the thesis less well than the top-ranked candidate.
Both flags reflect an elevated-volatility backdrop. Recent volatility is above its typical level, and the implied move is well above the typical realized move, so the premium paid is large.

critic.case_for: Microsoft beat both earnings and revenue estimates. The surrounding quarter showed strong cloud growth and a large rise in contracted future revenue. No recorded finding points the other way. Historically the stock closed higher in about 58% of 30-day periods. Post-earnings drift has long been documented as persisting after positive surprises. The next earnings report falls after expiration, so no company report can interrupt the window. The stock also held up far better than the technology sector over three months.

priced_in.reading: Since the beat became public, the stock has fallen 2.5%, which is 0.4 typical realized moves. The market has not rewarded the beat; the price moved against it. The size of that move is small relative to normal swings, so it reads as no follow-through rather than a decisive rejection.

critic.case_against: The stock has drifted down since the beat, so the market did not reward it. Recent research finds post-earnings drift in large caps has faded to almost nothing in 2025 and 2026. The thesis rests on a single moderately graded finding. A Fed decision falls inside the window, during an inverted, elevated volatility regime. Options bought after earnings tend to be overpriced. The call needs roughly a 3.8% rise just to break even.

loss_paths.title: Higher close, below breakeven
loss_paths.text: The stock can close above today's price yet below $521.40 at expiration. The call then loses part or all of its $2,140 cost. Only 56.3% of past higher-close periods were profitable for this strike.

loss_paths.title: Paying an inflated implied move
loss_paths.text: The implied move of 9.6% is 1.57 times the typical realized move. If the stock moves a normal amount, the call loses value as time passes and implied volatility settles.

loss_paths.title: Fed decision shock
loss_paths.text: The 9 December FOMC decision lands on day 20 of the hold. A hawkish surprise in an already falling tech sector could push the stock down before expiration.

missing.why_it_matters: Without the estimate revision history, there is no way to see whether analysts raised forecasts after the beat. Rising forecasts are what would sustain any drift.
Without quarterly consensus, the size of the surprise against current expectations cannot be confirmed independently, and the next quarter's bar cannot be judged.
The management discussion could carry forward commentary. The release says guidance was given only on the call and was not quoted.
Without macro expectations, there is no gauge of how the Fed decision and data releases inside the window might surprise.

dispositions.reason: The beat itself is recorded, and the filed earnings figure matches. As support for a higher close in 30 days it is weaker than stated: the price has slipped since the report, and recent evidence shows post-earnings drift has largely faded.

objections.title: The whole thesis rests on one moderately graded finding.
objections.text: No second, independent finding supports a higher close. The one that does is not graded as a primary source.

objections.title: The market has already moved against the beat.
objections.text: The stock is down 2.5% since the results. That is small in typical-move terms, but it is the opposite of follow-through.

objections.title: Post-earnings drift appears to have faded recently.
objections.text: Recent out-of-sample work shows the large-cap drift spread falling to about half a point for 2025 to 2026 announcements, measured over about 60 days rather than 30. That evidence is itself weakly graded.

objections.title: The option is expensive relative to normal movement.
objections.text: The implied move is well above the typical realized move. Research finds options bought after announcements are overpriced and retail option purchases lose on average. A correct direction can still lose money.

objections.title: A scheduled Fed decision sits inside the hold.
objections.text: The 9 December decision and several data releases fall before expiration. Volatility is elevated and the near-term curve is inverted.
